prize_parts.citation: For the theoretical prediction of the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 topological insulator, and its experimental observation in HgTe quantum wells.

statement.case_for: I have moved my preferred configuration from circuit QED (B038) to topological insulators (B006), and I want to say plainly why. After the first round, every colleague who commented on circuit QED raised the same two points: the 2025 prize already honoured the circuit platform within a year, and Girvin and Huang are missing from the credit. I argued that strong light-matter coupling is a different phenomenon from macroscopic tunnelling, and I still believe that on the physics. But the committee has to defend both the timing and the attribution, and I am the member with the strongest institutional stake in the subject (WACQT), so I should discount my own enthusiasm rather than ask colleagues to overcome their reservations. On the scientific merits, B006 has what I look for in a prize: a sharp prediction, the Kane-Mele Z2 invariant and helical edge states, followed by a decisive and quantitative measurement of quantized edge conductance in HgTe by Molenkamp's group, and about two decades of independent confirmation across materials and probes. It is a theory-plus-experiment pair of the clean kind I valued in circuit QED. I propose Kane, Mele and Molenkamp because the 2005 papers are one intellectual unit, and splitting Kane from Mele is the harder thing to defend; the citation is worded to the quantum spin Hall effect and its HgTe observation so that it states exactly what is credited and does not pretend to cover the 3D discovery.
statement.case_against: Three weaknesses remain, and I do not want to hide them. First, the allocation: choosing Mele leaves Hasan's three-dimensional ARPES discovery unrecognised, which is arguably the part with the broadest materials impact, and Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, who proposed the HgTe structure, are outside any three-name cut. Second, novelty relative to the 2016 prize; Danielsson and Mehlig make a good case that time-reversal-invariant topology in real materials is distinct from the quantum Hall and phase-transition work honoured then, but the citation has to make that distinction explicit. Third, I am outside my field here and defer to the condensed-matter colleagues on how the 2D and 3D credit divides. If the committee judges that omitting Hasan is not acceptable, I would rather see it settled openly than hidden in the wording.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that the 2016 prize rewarded topological phase transitions and the quantum Hall precedent, not the Z2 topological insulator or its observation in HgTe and 3D materials, and that a circuit QED prize would be distinct from 2025 in the same way, though he would want more time before a close successor.
responses.response: His point on 2016 persuades me: Thouless, Haldane and Kosterlitz did not cover time-reversal-invariant topology measured in real materials, and that closes the novelty objection I raised in round 1 well enough that I no longer treat it as a reason against. On circuit QED I accept his last remark; the parallel with 2025 is real in the committee's eyes even if the discoveries differ. Where I part from him is the third name. He proposes Hasan, which keeps the 3D discovery, but then Mele is separated from Kane on the very 2005 papers that define the theory. I do not think a theorist can be comfortable with that, and the experimental ARPES result, though important, rests on a 3D classification that came from a broader group of theorists. I would be willing to hear a different argument about what Hasan contributed that cannot be reached otherwise.

responses.point: Mehlig moved Mele into the preferred trio in place of Hasan, arguing that Kane and Mele are inseparable on the mechanism and that the 3D credit is diffuse because Fu, Kane, Mele, Moore, Balents and Roy all contributed, and he words the citation around the quantum spin Hall prediction and its HgTe observation.
responses.response: I now adopt his configuration and citation almost exactly. His reasoning on the diffuse 3D credit is the strongest answer I have seen to the chair's question about the third seat, because a prize that names Hasan for 3D raises an immediate question about the theorists who classified the 3D phase, whereas the 2D theory-plus-HgTe pair has a clean line from prediction to measurement. I would add one caution to his argument: it concedes that the broadest materials impact lies in the 3D case, so the committee should be honest that the citation recognises the quantum spin Hall effect specifically. I also note that he and I are in the same Gothenburg environment, as the chair's summary records, and I know of no collaboration that bears on this.

responses.point: Pearce supports B047 for a clean two-name credit, but states that B006 has the widest support and that, if the committee wants the widest consensus rather than the cleanest credit, B006 is the better fit at the price of the four-into-three problem; he also asks whether the Girvin credit gap is acceptable for B038.
responses.response: I answer his question honestly: no, I do not think the Girvin and Huang gap can be made comfortable under a three-name limit, and that is part of why I moved. I also take his framing that the committee is weighing breadth of support against cleanness of credit, but I would not let support counts decide the matter. B006 persuades me on science: it has the longest record of independent confirmation on the shortlist. The clock is a close second, and I keep it as an alternative. My remaining doubt about B047 is unchanged from round 1, that the committee must decide whether it is a new principle or a refinement of the 2005 and 2012 toolbox, and I am not the right person to decide that for atomic physics.

responses.point: Kroll argues that the lattice-clock credit is the cleanest on the list, that the magic-wavelength lattice is a genuine new principle, and that independent comparisons near 1e-18 meet his reproducibility standard; he also noted a loose WACQT tie with me and asked that both ties be disclosed.
responses.response: I agree on reproducibility and I agree that the credit for B047 is cleaner than for B006. The difference between us is how much weight to put on a null-result physics output so far; limits on constants and dark matter are valuable information, as he says, but I still read the lattice as an enabling concept, in the way the 2005 and 2012 prizes honoured tools. That is a judgment, not a criticism of the science. I confirm his note about WACQT: both of us have a link to Chalmers-led quantum technology, and I have disclosed that this concerns B038 and not B006 or B047. I keep his candidate as my first alternative on the metrology side if the committee prefers a prize with a plain two-name credit.

responses.point: Olsson prefers B006 but makes her support conditional on checking what Mele contributed in the 2005 papers, and says she would raise B038 only if the committee can answer the 2025 overlap and the Girvin and Huang gap convincingly.
responses.response: On her condition: the 2005 Kane-Mele papers contain the Z2 classification and the quantum spin Hall state as joint work, with Mele's contribution being part of the model and invariant rather than a side calculation, so I see no honest way to credit the prediction without him. I say this as a theorist outside condensed matter and would welcome her own check. On circuit QED, her statement that she would need a very clear answer on the 2025 overlap is fair, and after this round I do not think I can provide it convincingly, so I withdraw B038 as my preferred position.

uncertainties: Whether Mele versus Hasan is the right third seat, and whether the committee accepts that the 3D topological insulator discovery goes unrecognised.
Whether the citation wording on the quantum spin Hall effect and its HgTe observation answers the missing Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang credit and the 2016 prize.

Whether circuit QED (B038) would, after a few years and a possible broader credit that includes Girvin and Huang, be a better candidate than it is now; I may be discounting it too heavily out of caution about my own bias.
I am outside condensed matter and rely on colleagues for the 2D versus 3D credit judgment.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure: my conflicts concern B038, where I am a theorist in superconducting circuits at Chalmers and director of WACQT, and know Wallraff and Schoelkopf as peers; I have moved away from B038 as my preferred position and ask that my round-1 support for it be discounted. I have no known collaboration or institutional tie with Kane, Mele, Molenkamp, Hasan, Katori or Ye. Chalmers has hosted 2025 laureates, which is relevant to circuit-related candidates and not to B006. I note the shared WACQT link with Kroll and the Gothenburg environment shared with Mehlig and Olsson, without any known collaboration.
